theme: Idols vs. the living God; the linen loincloth
readingInstruction: Read Jeremiah 10:1-13:27. These chapters include a satire on idols, the covenant that was broken, Jeremiah’s first complaint, and two sign-acts: a linen loincloth and wine jars. Look for how God uses ordinary objects to teach.
settingTheScene: The setting continues in the reign of Jehoiakim. The people have been worshiping the gods of the surrounding nations, and Jeremiah mocks them. Chapters 11 and 12 reveal a personal crisis: his own village of Anathoth plots to kill him, and he asks God why the wicked prosper. Chapter 13 contains one of Jeremiah’s most visual sermons.
observation: “Their idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field, and they cannot speak” (10:5).
“But the LORD is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King” (10:10).
“It is he who made the earth by his power, who established the world by his wisdom” (10:12).
“Cursed be the man who does not hear the words of this covenant” (11:3).
“But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter” (11:19).
“Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why do all who are treacherous thrive?” (12:1).
“If you have raced with men on foot, and they have wearied you, how will you compete with horses?” (12:5).
“So I bought a loincloth… it was spoiled; it was good for nothing” (13:1-7).
interpretation:
Chapter 10 mocks the idols with a bit of humor. They are like scarecrows. They have to be carried because they cannot walk, and they cannot do good or harm. The contrast with the LORD is sharp: “There is none like you, O LORD.” The idols are made by hands. The LORD made the earth by his power. The call is to reverent fear before the King of the nations.

Chapter 11 turns to the covenant. The people heard the covenant words at Sinai and agreed, but then broke them. Jeremiah’s own townsmen of Anathoth plot to kill him if he does not stop prophesying. Then he opens a window into his heart. In chapter 12, he does what Habakkuk did: he complains to God. “Why does the way of the wicked prosper?” He wants answers. God does not give him a neat theology. He tells him that things will get harder. If racing with men on foot has worn him out, how will he cope with horses? God is preparing him for worse. It is not comforting, but it is honest. God does not coddle his servants.

Chapter 13 shows a sign. God tells Jeremiah to buy a linen loincloth, wear it, bury it by the Euphrates, and later dig it up. It is ruined. The meaning is that Israel was meant to cling to God like a loincloth to a man’s waist, “for a people, a name, a praise, and a glory.” But they would not listen, and so they became useless. The proud will be broken. The chapter ends with a question that pierces: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard his spots? Then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil.” Human nature cannot reform itself. Only God can change a heart, which is why the new covenant is so needed.
connection: Acts 14:15 and 17:22-31 draw on this critique of idols. Jesus was led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7; Acts 8:32). 1 Corinthians 8:4-6 says there is one God and one Lord, Jesus Christ. John 3:3-7 says no one can see the kingdom without being born again. Romans 7:18 says that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. Ezekiel 36:26 promises a new heart.
application:
Name any “scarecrow” idol in your life that cannot speak or act. Turn from it.

If you are weary, remember God’s honesty with Jeremiah: he prepares us for what is ahead.

Ask whether you cling to God like a loincloth, close and for his glory.
prayerPrompts: Praise God as the true, living God.
Confess where you have trusted scarecrows.
Ask him to strengthen you when you feel worn.
